views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Do not fire first with broad tariffs or offer purchase/structural concessions. Keep the WTO compensation track already opened on the solar and washer safeguards, and open talks with Washington—and with other WTO members—without new commitments. Hold a calibrated retaliation list in reserve if Section 301 or Section 232 produces China-specific duties, but do not escalate while the U.S. investigations are still unresolved.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but still prospective, not existential. The live dispute as of 1 March 2018 is an open Section 301 probe into IP and tech-transfer practices (initiated after the 14 August 2017 memorandum), a November 2017 Beijing visit that produced commercial MOUs but no structural IP concessions, and the 22 January 2018 Section 201 safeguards on solar panels and washing machines—China among the suppliers hit. MOFCOM called the safeguards an abuse of trade remedies and, in early February, sought WTO compensation consultations rather than a tariff volley. That is the right scale: solar is a flagship export industry, but it is not the export economy, FX stability, or regime legitimacy. Macro data confirm the dispute has not yet bitten: industrial production is running about 7% y/y, merchandise exports jumped in February, reserves remain above $3.1 trillion, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, and the yuan has strengthened (about 6.32 per dollar versus the mid-6.6s last autumn)—the opposite of FX stress. The larger risk is still off-stage: USTR has until August 2018 to decide 301, January reporting already floated large unilateral tariffs, and Commerce’s 16 February Section 232 options (including a 24% global steel tariff or a 53% levy on a list that includes China, plus aluminum options aimed at China) sit on the President’s desk with a mid-April clock. Escalating now would give Washington a pretext and could weld U.S. allies to a China-specific campaign just as DoD itself is arguing for targeting Chinese overcapacity rather than a global blast. Concession on Made in China 2025 / JV-licensing architecture would be premature: there is no matching U.S. offer and talks are not advanced. Negotiation without new commitments preserves the multilateral high ground, tests whether the November commercial channel can still buy time, and keeps options open if 301 or 232 actually fires.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer investigation is open; no finding or China-wide tariff list yet
Section 201 solar and washer safeguards already in force; China chose WTO compensation, not mirror tariffs
Section 232 steel/aluminum recommendations published 16 Feb 2018 but not yet decided
Chinese real economy still firm: IP ~7% y/y, strong exports, ample reserves, CNY appreciation
Nov 2017 Beijing visit showed U.S. appetite for commercial deals without structural IP concessions

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301. USTR investigation initiated.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit). First major tariff action of the administration.
China industrial production index 107.2 as of 2018-02-01 (about 7.2% y/y); change +1.0 over the window.
China merchandise exports $253.3bn in Feb 2018 (SA), up sharply over the window; dispute not yet visible in export volumes.
China reserves ex-gold about $3.15tn in Feb 2018; ample buffer, no reserve-drain signal.
CNY strengthened to 6.3183 per USD in Feb 2018 from 6.6254 in Oct 2017 (≈4.6% appreciation), not FX pressure.
MOFCOM's Wang Hejun: U.S. solar/washer decision is an 'abuse of trade remedy measures'; China expressed strong dissatisfaction and said it would work with other WTO members.
In early February 2018 China filed WTO complaints seeking compensation consultations on the solar and washer safeguards (G/SG/149 and G/SG/150).
Commerce 16 Feb 2018: steel/aluminum imports declared a national-security threat; options include 24% global steel tariff or 53% on a list including China; presidential decision due by mid-April.
5 Jan 2018: USTR 301 findings due by August 2018; reporting that the investigation may already be complete and large unilateral tariffs are under consideration.
MOFCOM on 301 initiation: U.S. use of domestic law rather than WTO is 'irresponsible' and criticism of China is 'not objective'; strong disapproval.
